traditions.name: Methodism
traditions.summary: A renewal movement within the Church of England led by John and Charles Wesley, which after Aldersgate (1738) and the start of field preaching (1739) organised converts into societies, classes and bands. American Methodists formed the Methodist Episcopal Church in 1784, and British Methodism separated from the Church of England after Wesley's death (1791). Methodism grew explosively on the American frontier and through mission in Africa, the Pacific and Asia. The United Methodist Church experienced a major schism over sexuality in 2019–2024.
distinctives: Prevenient grace and Arminian theology
Assurance of salvation through the witness of the Spirit
Christian perfection (entire sanctification) as a goal
Class meetings and connexional organisation
Hymns of Charles Wesley
Social holiness and itinerant preaching

profile.authority: Scripture as primary, read with tradition, reason and experience (the so-called Wesleyan Quadrilateral); Wesley's Sermons and Notes and the Articles of Religion as doctrinal standards.
profile.salvation: God's grace precedes, justifies and sanctifies; all may be saved, and believers can receive assurance and grow toward perfect love.
profile.sacraments: Baptism (including infants) and the Lord's Supper as means of grace; Wesley urged frequent communion.
profile.eschatology: Classical hope of Christ's return and judgment; nineteenth-century Methodism was often postmillennial and reform-minded.
profile.governance: Connexional: conferences appoint itinerant ministers; episcopal in American Methodism, conference-led in British Methodism.
profile.worship: Services of preaching and hymn singing with liturgy derived from the Book of Common Prayer; lovefeasts and watchnight services.

traditions.status: Active; c. 80 million in World Methodist Council member churches (2020).

traditions.name: Holiness Movement
traditions.summary: A nineteenth-century revival of Wesley's teaching on entire sanctification, popularised by Phoebe Palmer's Tuesday Meetings (from 1835) and camp meetings after the Civil War. Holiness preachers taught a definite 'second blessing' of heart purity after conversion, often called the baptism of the Holy Spirit. Tensions with mainstream Methodism led to new denominations such as the Wesleyan Methodists, Free Methodists, Church of the Nazarene (1908) and Church of God (Anderson); the movement directly prepared the ground for Pentecostalism.
distinctives: Entire sanctification as a second, instantaneous work of grace
'Altar theology' of consecration and faith (Phoebe Palmer)
Camp meetings and revival culture
Women preachers
Strict personal ethics (abstinence, plain dress)

profile.authority: Scripture, read through Wesleyan theology and confirmed in experience.
profile.salvation: Justification by faith followed by a second definite experience of entire sanctification that cleanses the heart from inbred sin.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and the Lord's Supper, often with flexibility on mode; less sacramental emphasis than early Methodism.
profile.eschatology: Initially postmillennial; many later Holiness groups adopted premillennialism.
profile.governance: Varied: episcopal, connexional or congregational denominations.
profile.worship: Revivalist services with testimonies, altar calls and gospel songs.

traditions.status: Active in denominations such as the Church of the Nazarene (c. 2.6 million members) and the Free Methodist and Wesleyan churches.

traditions.name: The Salvation Army
traditions.summary: Founded in London's East End in 1865 by William and Catherine Booth as the Christian Mission, renamed The Salvation Army in 1878 with a military structure of officers and soldiers. It combines Holiness evangelism with extensive social work among the poor, the homeless and addicts. It does not practise sacraments, believing them non-essential to salvation. Present in over 130 countries, it is one of the world's largest charitable organisations.
distinctives: Military structure, uniforms and ranks
No sacraments of baptism or communion
Holiness doctrine of sanctification
Women officers and preachers from the outset
Large-scale social services and disaster relief

profile.authority: Scripture and the Army's eleven Articles of Faith.
profile.salvation: Repentance toward God, faith in Christ and regeneration by the Holy Spirit, followed by the privilege of entire sanctification.
profile.sacraments: No outward sacraments; soldiers are enrolled under the flag and emphasise an inward, sacramental life.
profile.eschatology: Christ's return, resurrection, judgment and eternal reward or punishment.
profile.governance: Hierarchical, led by an elected General and commissioned officers.
profile.worship: Informal meetings with brass bands, songs, testimonies and a 'mercy seat' for prayer.

traditions.status: Active; c. 1.5 million soldiers and adherents in over 130 countries.

traditions.name: Evangelicalism
traditions.summary: A transdenominational Protestant movement that emerged from the eighteenth-century awakenings of Edwards, Whitefield and Wesley. David Bebbington characterises it by conversionism, activism, biblicism and crucicentrism. Evangelicals drove missions, abolition and social reform in the nineteenth century; in the twentieth, figures such as Billy Graham and John Stott and the Lausanne Movement (1974) shaped a global identity distinct from fundamentalism. It now spans denominations and independent churches worldwide, with most adherents in the Global South.
distinctives: Conversionism: the need for personal conversion
Biblicism: high regard for the Bible's authority
Crucicentrism: focus on Christ's atoning death
Activism: evangelism and social engagement
Parachurch organisations and global mission networks

profile.authority: The Bible as the inspired and authoritative (often 'inerrant' or 'infallible') Word of God.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through personal faith in Christ's substitutionary atonement, usually experienced as being 'born again'.
profile.sacraments: Varies by denomination: infant or believer's baptism; the Lord's Supper commonly seen as memorial or spiritual presence.
profile.eschatology: Diverse; premillennialism (including dispensationalism) widespread in North America, amillennialism and postmillennialism elsewhere.
profile.governance: Denominational polity varies; many independent and nondenominational churches.
profile.worship: Preaching-centred services with contemporary or traditional music; strong emphasis on personal devotion.

traditions.status: Active; c. 285 million evangelicals (Pew 2010 estimate); definitions and counts vary widely.

traditions.name: Stone–Campbell Restoration Movement
traditions.summary: An American movement seeking Christian unity by restoring the New Testament church, led by former Presbyterians Barton W. Stone (associated with the Cane Ridge revival, 1801) and Thomas and Alexander Campbell. The Stone 'Christians' and Campbell 'Disciples' united in 1832, rejecting creeds as tests of fellowship. Disputes over instrumental music and missionary societies divided the movement into the Churches of Christ (a cappella), the Christian Churches/Churches of Christ, and the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ).
distinctives: 'No creed but Christ, no book but the Bible'
Restoration of New Testament patterns of church life
Believer's baptism by immersion for the remission of sins
Weekly Lord's Supper
Christian unity as a central goal

profile.authority: The New Testament as the pattern for the church, read with common-sense rationality; creeds rejected as tests of fellowship.
profile.salvation: Faith, repentance, confession and baptism by immersion for the forgiveness of sins.
profile.sacraments: Ordinances: believer's baptism by immersion and weekly communion.
profile.eschatology: Diverse; early Campbell was postmillennial, many later Churches of Christ amillennial.
profile.governance: Congregational, with elders and deacons; the Disciples have regional and general structures.
profile.worship: Weekly communion at the centre; Churches of Christ sing without instruments.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon, with stress on the New Testament.

traditions.status: Active; c. 5 million members across its three main streams worldwide.

traditions.name: Seventh-day Adventist Church
traditions.summary: A Protestant church that emerged from William Miller's Adventist movement after the Great Disappointment of 1844, when Christ did not return as expected. Led by Joseph Bates, James White and Ellen G. White, whose writings are regarded as inspired counsel, believers adopted the seventh-day Sabbath and a doctrine of Christ's heavenly sanctuary ministry. Organised formally in 1863, it is known for health reform, education and medical mission, and is now one of the most widespread Protestant denominations, with most members in Africa and Latin America. It holds Trinitarian doctrine.
distinctives: Saturday (seventh-day) Sabbath observance
Imminent, literal Second Coming
Investigative judgment and the heavenly sanctuary (from 1844)
Conditional immortality and annihilation of the wicked
Health message and vegetarian lifestyle
Ellen G. White's prophetic ministry

profile.authority: Scripture alone as the standard of faith; Ellen G. White's writings regarded as a continuing, authoritative source of truth subordinate to the Bible.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, with obedience to God's commandments, including the Sabbath, as the fruit of faith.
profile.sacraments: Ordinances of believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper preceded by footwashing.
profile.eschatology: Historicist premillennialism: Christ's visible return, a millennium in heaven, then final destruction of the wicked and a renewed earth.
profile.governance: Representative: local churches, conferences, unions, divisions and the General Conference.
profile.worship: Sabbath School and divine service on Saturday; quarterly communion with footwashing.

traditions.name: Pentecostalism
traditions.summary: A movement emphasising the baptism in the Holy Spirit, evidenced by speaking in tongues, and the restoration of spiritual gifts such as healing and prophecy. With roots in the Holiness movement and Charles Parham's teaching (Topeka, 1901), it spread worldwide from William J. Seymour's interracial Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles (1906–1909); parallel revivals arose in India (Mukti, 1905), Korea, Chile and elsewhere. Pentecostalism grew to become one of the largest Christian movements, especially in Latin America, Africa and Asia.
distinctives: Baptism in the Holy Spirit as an experience subsequent to conversion
Speaking in tongues (often as 'initial evidence')
Divine healing and spiritual gifts
Expressive, participatory worship
Strong expectation of Christ's return and urgent evangelism

profile.authority: Scripture as the inspired Word of God, read in expectation that the experiences of Acts continue today.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, followed by Spirit baptism for empowerment; 'full gospel' of Christ as Saviour, Sanctifier, Spirit-baptiser, Healer and Coming King.
profile.sacraments: Ordinances of believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper; footwashing in some churches.
profile.eschatology: Mostly premillennial, often dispensational, with intense expectation of Christ's imminent return.
profile.governance: Varied: congregational, presbyterian-style fellowships and episcopal denominations.
profile.worship: Spontaneous, exuberant worship with raised hands, tongues, prophecy, prayer for healing and altar calls.

traditions.status: Active; c. 279 million classical Pentecostals in 2010 (Pew); with charismatics, over 580 million.

traditions.name: Assemblies of God
traditions.summary: The largest Pentecostal denomination, organised at Hot Springs, Arkansas, in 1914 by ministers seeking cooperation and doctrinal order among independent Pentecostal churches. It adopted the Statement of Fundamental Truths in 1916, affirming the Trinity after the Oneness controversy. Through extensive missions, national Assemblies of God churches grew rapidly, notably in Brazil (where a separate movement began in 1911), Nigeria and South Korea, home of Yoido Full Gospel Church.
distinctives: Spirit baptism with tongues as initial physical evidence
Trinitarian Pentecostalism (Statement of Fundamental Truths, 1916)
Divine healing in the atonement
Cooperative fellowship of self-governing national churches
Strong missionary emphasis

profile.authority: The Scriptures as the inspired, infallible and authoritative Word of God.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through repentance and faith in Christ; Spirit baptism as a distinct subsequent empowerment.
profile.sacraments: Ordinances of water baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial, with the imminent rapture of the church, Christ's millennial reign and final judgment.
profile.governance: Cooperative: congregational local churches in district councils and national General Councils, linked by the World Assemblies of God Fellowship.
profile.worship: Pentecostal worship with contemporary music, spiritual gifts and prayer for healing.

traditions.status: Active; c. 69 million adherents worldwide (World Assemblies of God Fellowship estimate).

traditions.name: Oneness Pentecostalism
traditions.summary: A branch of Pentecostalism that arose from the 'New Issue' at the Arroyo Seco camp meeting (1913), when teachers such as R. E. McAlister and Frank Ewart urged baptism 'in the name of Jesus' only. It teaches that God is one person who manifests as Father, Son and Spirit, rejecting the doctrine of three persons and so standing outside historic Nicene orthodoxy (its adherents see it as restoring apostolic faith). Major bodies include the United Pentecostal Church International (1945), and Oneness churches are strong in Latin America, Ethiopia and China (the True Jesus Church).
distinctives: God as one being and one person, revealed in Jesus
Baptism in the name of Jesus only
New birth as repentance, Jesus-name baptism and Spirit baptism with tongues
Holiness standards of dress and conduct in many churches

profile.authority: Scripture as the inspired Word of God, with emphasis on Acts 2:38 as the pattern of salvation.
profile.salvation: Repentance, water baptism in Jesus' name and receiving the Holy Spirit with tongues together constitute the new birth.
profile.sacraments: Ordinances of Jesus-name baptism by immersion, the Lord's Supper and often footwashing.
profile.governance: Varied; the UPCI has district and general conferences with congregational local churches.
profile.worship: Pentecostal worship with tongues, healing and exuberant praise.

traditions.status: Active; estimates range from c. 20 to 30 million adherents worldwide; outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.

traditions.name: Charismatic Renewal
traditions.summary: The spread of Pentecostal-style experience of the Holy Spirit within historic churches, beginning publicly when Episcopal priest Dennis Bennett announced his Spirit baptism in Van Nuys, California (1960). It spread through Lutheran, Presbyterian, Anglican and Orthodox circles, and from the Duquesne Weekend (1967) into Catholicism, where the Catholic Charismatic Renewal received papal encouragement. Charismatics generally remained in their denominations, integrating gifts of the Spirit with their own theology and sacramental life.
distinctives: Baptism in (or release of) the Spirit within existing churches
Spiritual gifts: tongues, prophecy, healing
Prayer groups and covenant communities
Contemporary praise and worship music
Ecumenical cooperation across traditions

profile.authority: Each participant's church tradition (Scripture, creeds, magisterium) combined with openness to the Spirit's present activity.
profile.salvation: Follows the host tradition's soteriology; Spirit baptism understood as renewal of grace already received (e.g. in baptism and confirmation).
profile.sacraments: As in the host tradition; Catholic charismatics retain the seven sacraments.
profile.governance: Renewal networks and service committees within existing church structures.
profile.worship: Prayer meetings with praise, tongues, prophecy and healing alongside traditional liturgies.

traditions.status: Active; c. 305 million charismatics in 2010 (Pew), the majority Catholic.

traditions.name: Neo-charismatic and Independent Churches
traditions.summary: A broad 'third wave' category for independent and post-denominational churches with Pentecostal-charismatic spirituality that are neither classical Pentecostal nor part of renewal in historic churches. It includes the Vineyard movement (John Wimber), networks such as Hillsong and Bethel, many Nigerian, Brazilian and Korean megachurches, and the New Apostolic Reformation associated with C. Peter Wagner. Some streams emphasise power evangelism, apostolic networks or the prosperity gospel, which other Christians strongly criticise.
distinctives: Signs and wonders and 'power evangelism'
Independent networks and megachurches
Contemporary worship music industry
Apostolic and prophetic leadership in some streams
Prosperity teaching in some (contested) streams

profile.authority: Scripture, with strong openness to present-day prophetic words and apostolic leadership.
profile.salvation: Evangelical faith in Christ, with expectation of healing, deliverance and empowerment.
profile.sacraments: Believer's baptism and communion, usually as ordinances.
profile.eschatology: Varied; some hold dominion or 'kingdom now' views, others classical premillennialism.
profile.governance: Often founder-led or apostolic networks rather than denominations.
profile.worship: Extended contemporary worship sets, ministry times with prayer for healing and prophecy.

traditions.status: Active; among the fastest-growing Christian groups (hundreds of millions by WCD's broad definitions).

traditions.name: African Initiated Churches
traditions.summary: Churches founded by Africans rather than by missionaries, beginning with 'Ethiopian' churches that broke from mission control in the 1880s–1890s, such as Mangena Mokone's Ethiopian Church in Pretoria (1892). Prophet-healing movements followed: the Harrist churches (West Africa, 1913), the Kimbanguist church (Congo, 1921), Aladura churches in Nigeria, and Zionist and Apostolic churches in southern Africa, including the Zion Christian Church. They integrate African cultural forms with the Bible, emphasising healing, prophecy and protection from evil.
distinctives: African leadership and cultural expression
Prophetic founders and healing ministries
Use of holy water, robes and sacred sites
Attention to dreams, visions and spiritual protection
Some practise polygamy-tolerant or Old Testament-influenced customs

profile.authority: Scripture, often read alongside the revelations of prophet-founders and the guidance of the Spirit.
profile.salvation: Salvation in Christ understood holistically: forgiveness, healing, protection and well-being.
profile.sacraments: Baptism (often by immersion in rivers), communion and many healing rituals.
profile.eschatology: Varied; some expect a new Jerusalem centred on holy cities such as Moria or Nkamba.
profile.governance: Often led by prophet-founders and their successors, with bishops or archbishops.
profile.worship: Vibrant worship with drums, dance, prayer for healing and white robes.
profile.canon: The Protestant canon; some churches add founders' hymns or writings.

traditions.status: Active; tens of millions of members (estimates often exceed 60 million).

traditions.name: Chinese House Churches
traditions.summary: Unregistered Protestant congregations in the People's Republic of China that refused to join the state-sanctioned Three-Self Patriotic Movement (1954). Drawing on indigenous movements such as Watchman Nee's Little Flock and Wang Mingdao's independent church, they survived the Cultural Revolution in secret and grew dramatically from the late 1970s, especially in rural Henan and Anhui and later among urban professionals. They have faced recurrent crackdowns, including the closure of Chengdu's Early Rain Covenant Church in 2018.
distinctives: Independence from state registration
Theology shaped by persecution and suffering
Lay leadership and itinerant evangelists
Indigenous Chinese hymnody (e.g. the Canaan Hymns)
Evangelical and often Pentecostal-influenced piety

profile.authority: Scripture as the supreme authority, interpreted largely through evangelical and indigenous Chinese traditions.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, with strong emphasis on conversion and holy living.
profile.sacraments: Baptism (often of believers) and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Often premillennial; some networks promote the 'Back to Jerusalem' missionary vision.
profile.governance: Independent congregations and large rural networks; urban churches increasingly Reformed or presbyterian.
profile.worship: Small home gatherings with prayer, Bible study and singing.

traditions.status: Active; estimates of membership range widely, from c. 30 million to over 60 million.

traditions.name: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
traditions.summary: Founded by Joseph Smith in 1830 in New York state, it emerged from the same restorationist milieu as the Stone–Campbell movement, teaching that the true church had been lost in a 'Great Apostasy' and restored through new revelation. Its scriptures include the Book of Mormon alongside the Bible. After Smith's death (1844) most members followed Brigham Young to Utah. Its doctrine of God, which describes the Father, Son and Holy Ghost as three distinct beings, places it outside historic Nicene orthodoxy, although members regard themselves as Christians.
distinctives: Restoration of priesthood authority and prophetic leadership
Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants and Pearl of Great Price as scripture
Godhead of three distinct beings
Temple ordinances, including eternal marriage and baptism for the dead
Extensive lay ministry and missionary service

profile.authority: The Bible 'as far as it is translated correctly', the Book of Mormon and other modern scriptures, and continuing revelation through living prophets and apostles.
profile.salvation: Salvation through the atonement of Jesus Christ, received by faith, repentance, baptism, the gift of the Holy Ghost and enduring to the end; exaltation requires temple covenants.
profile.sacraments: Ordinances: baptism by immersion at age eight or older, confirmation, the weekly sacrament (bread and water) and temple ordinances.
profile.eschatology: Christ's Second Coming and millennial reign, resurrection, and a final judgment assigning people to degrees of glory.
profile.governance: Hierarchical: President (prophet), First Presidency and Quorum of the Twelve Apostles; lay bishops lead wards.
profile.worship: Sunday sacrament meetings in chapels; temple worship for members in good standing.
profile.canon: The Bible (King James Version in English), Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants and Pearl of Great Price.

traditions.status: Active; c. 17.5 million members (2024); outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.

traditions.name: Jehovah's Witnesses
traditions.summary: A movement that grew from the Bible Student circles of Charles Taze Russell, who was influenced by Adventist thinkers and began publishing Zion's Watch Tower in 1879. Under Joseph Rutherford it adopted the name Jehovah's Witnesses (1931). Witnesses teach that Jehovah alone is almighty God, that Jesus is God's first creation and that the Holy Spirit is God's active force, positions outside historic Nicene orthodoxy. Known for door-to-door evangelism, refusal of blood transfusions and political neutrality, Witnesses have faced persecution, including in Nazi Germany and modern Russia.
distinctives: Use of the divine name Jehovah
Jesus as God's first creation; denial of the Trinity
Door-to-door and public witnessing
Refusal of blood transfusions, military service and political involvement
Expectation of Armageddon and an earthly paradise

profile.authority: The Bible (New World Translation) as interpreted by the Governing Body, regarded as the 'faithful and discreet slave'.
profile.salvation: Salvation through faith in Christ's ransom sacrifice and faithful obedience; 144,000 anointed go to heaven, while a 'great crowd' inherits paradise on earth.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion as a symbol of dedication, and an annual Memorial of Christ's death (partaken only by those claiming to be anointed).
profile.eschatology: Imminent Armageddon, Christ's thousand-year reign, resurrection to a restored earth and annihilation of the wicked; no hellfire.
profile.governance: Centralised under the Governing Body; congregations led by appointed elders and ministerial servants.
profile.worship: Meetings in Kingdom Halls for Bible study, instruction and song; no clergy class.
profile.canon: The 66-book canon in the New World Translation.

traditions.status: Active; c. 8.8 million active publishers (2023); outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.
